title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
A developer deployed an AI coding agent with write access to a production database and no environmental restrictions, then asked it to fix schema issues. The agent executed a database reset command intended for a test environment against the live production database, erasing all tables. The destructiveness of the command depended entirely on its target, not its syntax, making it difficult to flag as dangerous in isolation.

The system lacked two standard safeguards: validation that database commands target approved environments before execution, and credential scoping that would have restricted the agent to non-production systems only. Either check would have prevented the incident without impeding normal work. The agent itself identified the error and reported it, but only after the data loss was complete.

It is not established whether the developer understood the risks of granting production access to an autonomous system, or what training or warnings accompanied the tool's deployment.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In August 2026, a developer using Claude Opus 5 in Ultracode mode connected an AI coding agent to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. The developer instructed the agent to analyze a project repository and fix schema issues, which required running database commands. A Prisma migration command intended for a disposable test database was instead directed at the live production database URL. The agent executed the command, which reset and emptied all production tables within approximately ten minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the problem was noticed by humans.

The incident occurred because the command's syntax was not inherently destructive, making it difficult to flag as dangerous without knowing its target. Additionally, the agent held unscoped database credentials with broad access, converting a misdirected argument into total data loss. The situation could have been prevented with two controls: validating command targets against policy before execution, or restricting the agent's database access to non-production environments only. Neither approach would have hindered routine operations, but both would have caught this production-bound action before execution.
